 The Seattle minimum wage will increase next year, but it's still not high enough
 By 
 Annabelle Scott The Daily 
 Nov 16, 2026, 2:00 PM
 Seattle just announced it will be raising its minimum wage in 2027 from $21.30 to $22.14 an hour. It’s good that it’s going up, but is the 84-cent change really enough? 
 As someone from the Deep South, the minimum wage here is unheard of. I am from Georgia, where the minimum wage is $5.15 per hour, meaning it defaults to the federal minimum wage of $7.25 per hour. I once worked for that meager amount, and while the paychecks were depressing, I was working part-time to save up for college and occasional outings with my friends, not for survival.
 If you are making above $20 per hour in Georgia at my age, you’re making an impressive amount of money. It is nearly impossible to find a job that offers that much in the rural-suburban area where I am from. For plenty of states in the United States, it’s similar.
 Considering all of this, you would think that I am jumping up and down at the thought of making the Seattle minimum wage. But just because the bar was lowered for me originally does not mean I will accept an amount that is still not enough to afford to live in Seattle. 
 I think many can agree that the federal minimum wage is not enough to survive off of, but, despite the $14 difference, the Seattle minimum wage is not much better. Considering the living expenses of the city, it is not nearly enough. 
 Rebecca Conway is a third-year student and works for minimum wage at The Little Gym in Maple Leaf, Seattle as a gymnastics instructor. Her work can be difficult and working minimum wage can feel like improper consolation. 
 “I mean, I obviously wish I got paid more. I work with kids, so the age group I work with is like 2 to 5 year olds. So it's a lot of mental energy required,” Conway said.
 Conway also worked a minimum wage job in North Carolina, her home state, before moving to Seattle for school. The minimum wage in North Carolina is $7.25 per hour. When comparing her two jobs, Conway pointed out the difference in cost of living between the two states. 
 “I feel like it's kind of hard to compare because places like that, the cost of living is so much lower, so it's more proportional, I guess, but I appreciate the Seattle minimum wage for sure,” Conway said. 
 Despite enjoying the Seattle minimum wage, Conway agreed that it should be raised. 
 Advertisement 
 “I feel like the cost of living is just so high here, and I don't see how anyone could live on their own, for gas, food, a nice place to live in the same area without roommates or anything,” Conway said. “Like, there's no way someone can afford that on minimum wage.” 
 This summer, I was able to work in Virginia, once again for minimum wage, but a slight upgrade of $12.77 an hour. I also had a second job making $20 an hour. Despite saving up all summer, I still don’t have enough money to support myself on my own in Seattle without picking up a job while also studying. 
 Needing multiple jobs to simply survive should not be the norm. 
 From the older generation, I have heard plenty of complaints about Gen Z’s work ethic. News outlets like Fox News never fail to mention how lazy Gen Z is, blaming the high unemployment rates on our work ethic rather than the job market and unlivable wages.
 These critiques beg the question: Why should people have to overextend themselves to the point of exhaustion to simply survive? This should not be normalized. Living paycheck to paycheck is not sustainable and shouldn’t be considered survival. 
 Survival is more than being able to put food on the table, pay your bills, your rent, and any other physical expense. Survival means being able to at least have the option of mental wellbeing on top of that, which is not possible if you’re required to work multiple jobs to get by. It is not possible if you can’t afford to spend time with friends now and then. It is not possible if you have to weigh which meals you can afford to eat each day. 
 It’s good that Seattle is increasing the minimum wage, but it is critical that we start to consider if this change is anywhere near enough. A real increase in the Seattle minimum wage would begin to make survival possible for Seattle citizens and would ensure workers are fairly compensated for their work. 
 The Seattle minimum wage has been on an upwards trajectory for years, hopefully this increase will spark further increases in the near future.
